title: Four Companies Named as H-1B 'Willful Violators' as Labor Department Steps Up Enforcement
excerpt: The Department of Labor has updated its list of employers barred from the H-1B program, naming four companies as willful violators, while launching 'Project Firewall' to intensify compliance investigations across the tech industry.
body:
• The U.S. Department of Labor's updated H-1B debarment list names four companies — GowraTech, Renotek Group, Seeloz, and Sherwood Academy — as willful violators barred from sponsoring H-1B workers for two years each.
  • A separate willful violator list maintained by the DOL's Wage and Hour Division identifies 13 employers found to have deliberately violated H-1B program rules.
  • Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer has launched 'Project Firewall,' a new enforcement initiative targeting H-1B program abuse with on-site audits and inter-agency investigations.
  • Major tech companies including Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta face heightened compliance scrutiny as the administration combines fee increases with enforcement crackdowns.

The Updated Blacklist

The Department of Labor has updated its list of employers disqualified from participating in the H-1B visa program, effective July 1, 2026. Four companies are currently barred as willful violators:

GowraTech, LLC, debarred from May 2025 through May 2027; Renotek Group LLC, barred from August 2025 through August 2027; Seeloz, Inc., debarred from March 2026 through March 2028; and Sherwood at Mount Dora, Inc., doing business as Sherwood Academy, the most recent addition, barred from May 2026 through May 2028.

A separate willful violator list maintained by the DOL's Wage and Hour Division contains 13 employers found to have deliberately broken H-1B program rules, including wage violations and fraudulent labor condition applications. Companies on this list face stricter scrutiny for up to five years and must meet additional requirements when filing future visa applications.

Project Firewall: A New Enforcement Posture

The updated lists come as the Labor Department launches what it calls "Project Firewall," a new enforcement initiative that immigration attorneys say marks a major posture change for the agency.

"They're going to be combing through everything, using the full force of the federal government to make a big splash for anyone who they believe is not playing by the rules."

— Christopher Thomas, partner at Holland & Hart LLP

Under the initiative, companies that have used the H-1B program to attract foreign talent — including Amazon, Microsoft, Walmart, and Meta — can expect new compliance investigations from the DOL. The investigations will be approved personally by Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer and will include on-site visits from Wage and Hour officers.

Employers found with discrepancies in record-keeping or worker pay could face tens of thousands of dollars in civil penalties or outright debarment from the program. The DOL is also working with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, the Justice Department, and USCIS on enforcement coordination.

What Triggers a Violation

H-1B employers must submit a certified labor condition application and maintain a "public access file" at each work site containing information about the guest worker's wage and how it complies with prevailing wage regulations. Federal law mandates that hiring a visa worker must not negatively impact the pay and working conditions of U.S. citizen employees.

Common violations include "benching" — placing H-1B workers in nonproductive status without pay — and failing to pay the required prevailing wage. In a recent case, IT services company Cigniti Technologies was found to have benched an employee for 15 months, resulting in $64,244 in recovered wages.

Yet critics note the disconnect between the administration's rhetoric about widespread abuse and the actual enforcement record. According to the DOL's own website, only five employers have been banned in the last two years. "If there is so much abuse, why aren't more people being debarred?" asked Charles Kuck, managing partner of Kuck Baxter Immigration.

Impact on Indian IT Workers

Indian nationals represent the single largest group of H-1B visa holders, and many work through the staffing and IT services firms that face the most scrutiny under Project Firewall. The enhanced enforcement creates both risks and protections: workers at non-compliant firms could see their employment disrupted, but the DOL offers whistleblower protections for H-1B holders who report violations.

Immigration attorneys warn the combined effect of fee increases and enforcement crackdowns is pushing some companies to reconsider staffing positions in the United States entirely. "Companies are thinking that maybe they shouldn't be staffing these positions in the United States at all," said Christopher Thomas of Holland & Hart.

What's Next

The administration plans to raise the H-1B prevailing wage structure through a DOL rule aimed at limiting the use of visas to undercut American wages. DHS has also signaled plans to revamp the H-1B lottery to prioritize highly-skilled, highly-paid foreign workers. Both initiatives echo measures from Trump's first term that were blocked by federal courts for bypassing required rulemaking procedures.
